newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Thyssen, Veba deny Vulkan report.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thyssen, Veba deny Vulkan report.

text.p: German industrial groups Thyssen AG and Veba AG denied a report on Wednesday that they were interested in taking over bankrupt shipyard group Bremer Vulkan Verbund AG.

The business daily Handelsblatt said on its front page that the two companies, while distancing themselves from takeover speculation, wanted to pick up loss carryovers totalling three billion to four billion marks ($1.7-$2.3 billion) to cut their tax exposure.
"Veba sharply denies newspaper reports that it is interested in a takeover of Bremer Vulkan AG ... There is absolutely nothing in it," Veba said in a statement
Thyssen issued its denial already on Tuesday when it commented on a report in the Weser Kurier, a Bremen newspaper, that it wanted to buy Vulkan.
Jobst Wellensiek, the receiver for Bremer Vulkan since it collapsed a year ago, told Reuters that he was extremely sceptical about the Handelsblatt report and considered a takeover unlikely.
Normally, such a takeover would be preceded by weeks of discussions with the receiver, but no one had contacted him, Wellensiek said. "This public discussion doesn't fit the picture," he said.

He added that the newspaper's estimate of three to four billion marks in losses at Bremer Vulkan was too high. That figure represented claims against the shipbuilder, but the actual losses were about 2.5 billion marks, he said.
Equities analysts found the possibility of a takeover intriguing, but said it would be legally difficult.
"The tax-loss carry-forwards are certainly an asset for a potential buyer. Vulkan wasn't able to make use of them because of a lack of profit," said analyst Olaf Toelke at Merrill Lynch in London.

Handelsblatt said Thyssen, which wants to refocus on its core steel and engineering, was planning to sell its E-Plus mobile telephone unit -- a move which would lead to sizeable extraordinary earnings.

To cut its tax exposure, Thyssen could offset the windfall gain from the E-Plus sale by offsetting it with the Vulkan loss carryover. Telecommunications venture o.tel.o, which is owned by utilities Veba and RWE AG, has been named as a potential buyer for E-Plus.
But Toelke said German law would allow the Vulkan losses to be used to offset only German domestic operating profits, and probably only in the shipbuilding or machinery sectors.

A buyer would need to negotiate with tax authorities for permission to use the losses to offset extraordinary gains, but that would appear extremely unlikely in this case given the German government's current fiscal straits and the background of the Bremer Vulkan collapse.
"It would be asking the authorities to subsidise the Bremer Vulkan losses a second time," Toelke said.

The Handelsblatt quoted informed sources as saying that the two potential buyers wanted to dampen takeover talk to prevent shares in Bremer Vulkan -- which are still listed -- from jumping further after their price trebled on Monday.
Bremer Vulkan shares were trading on Wednesday at 7.40 marks, up from Tuesday's close of 5.10 marks. On Monday they had surged to 9.90 marks from 3.44 marks last Friday.

That is still a far from the level of around 80 marks where they were trading a year ago. The Bremen shipbuilder collapsed after it emerged that managers had misused European Union industrial subsidies to prop up the company.

Ulrich Noelle, finance senator for the city state of Bremen, confirmed at the weekend that he was talking to two potential buyers. Handelsblatt said in its report, however, that Noelle had distanced himself from such plans.
One member of the committee of creditors to Vulkan, Joerg Stein, told Handelsblatt that a sale of the group to the two potential buyers would be "sensible, wise and achievable".
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-2609750 ($ = 1.724 German Marks)
